body:
Usage scenario:
* A webapp that displays HTML emails, posts, comments, or chat messages from untrusted people. That might be a webmail, web discussion forum, chat with other users, or ratings below a product. Many webapps have such functionality these days, in some form or variation.

Goal:
* Hacks of the users (RCE) are unacceptable. Not even 1 hack in 10 years.

Facts:
* Browsers have multiple critical security holes (RCE - remote code execution), _every month_.
* RCE is worse than XSS
* Navigation is part of the web
  * Users click on links
  * Running arbitary URL schemes can lead to RCEs E.g. [CVE-2010-1885](https://www.cvedetails.com/cve/CVE-2010-1885/), [CVE-2022-30190](https://www.cvedetails.com/cve/CVE-2022-30190/), ...

Threat model:
1. Take arbitary hostile HTML from an attacker (think: Russian hacker) that's included in a spear phishing email directed at the user
2. Run that HTML through the sanitizer
3. Include that sanitized HTML into the web mail app or the Thunderbird HTML UI or a web forum or BlueSky or whatever other app. For the sake of the threat model, the app (e.g. Thunderbird) has local execution rights. *1
4. Render that sanitized HTML, including links and inline images
5. The user clicks on links, or replies to the email
6. There must be no way for the attacker to
   a) modify parts of the mail user agent user interface (XSS) or
   b) do actions on behalf of the user (XSS) or
   c) run code with OS user priviledges (remote code execution, RCE).
7. The above must hold true (secure) in the face of yet unknown security holes in the browser/HTML engine. 0 RCEs in the coming 10 years, excluding bugs in image decoders.

*1) This is nonewithstanding the argument whether this is wise or not. This definition is for this particular threat model. Defense in depth means that the app might have other defenses, but defense in depth also means that each layer *on its own* must hold back the waters. This is the only way to succeed, and even that is risky, as proven every year when BlackHat p0wns Chrome despite its multiple nested sandboxes.

So, browser defenses are insufficient. The purpose of the sanitizer is to catch attacks that the browser otherwise would let through.

Security research has consistently and regularly shown that this additional multi-level protection in depth is necessary and indispensible.

Given that there's a finite number of elements and attributes that allow for linking functionality, is there any reason why such an "unknown scheme link remover" couldn't be built in userland, after running the HTML through the sanitizer? Unlike say a dangling markup attack, unknown schemes aren't harmful until clicked on/activated, right?

Let's not discuss any of that here. Marking comments as off-topic therefore. This issue is specifically to document the threat models for `setHTML()` with an empty sanitizer and the threat model for the "`default`" sanitizer, as also discussed in the document I referenced.
